¶
'''brook-mint''' (bru̇k′mint), ''n.'' [< AS. ''brōcminte'', < ''brōc'', brook, + ''minte'', mint.] The water-mint, ''Mentha sylvestris.''

'''brook-moss''' (bru̇k′môs), ''n.'' A name given to species of the genus ''Dichelyma'', slender aquatic mosses, with elongated leaves in three ranks, and with the fruit on short lateral branches.

'''brookweed''' (bru̇k′wēd), ''n.'' A plant, the water-pimpernel, ''Samolus Valerandi.'' See ''Samolus.''

'''brooky''' (bru̇k′i), ''a.'' [< ''brook''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Abounding with brooks: as, “Hebron’s ''brooky'' sides,” ''J. Dyer'', The Fleece, ii.

'''broom'''<sup>1</sup> (bröm), ''n.'' [< ME. ''broom'', ''brom'', broom (the plant, L. ''genista'') (also applied to the tamarisk, L. ''myrica''), a brush, < AS. ''brōm'' = MD. ''broem'' (cf. MLG. ''brām'', LG. ''braam''), broom (L. ''genista''): see ''bramble.''] '''1.''' The popular name of several plants, mostly leguminous shrubs, characterized by long, slender branches and numerous yellow flowers. {{smaller|The common or Irish broom is the ''Cytisus'' (''Genista'') ''scoparius'', abundant throughout Europe, and famous as the ''planta genista'' (French ''plante genêt'') which was the badge of the Plantagenets. It is a valuable remedy in dropsy, being one of the most efficient of hydragogues, and its seeds are used as a substitute for coffee. Spanish broom (''Spartium junceum'') is a closely allied species, as is also the dyer’s broom (''Genista tinctoria''), which was formerly much used as a yellow dye and as the basis of the once celebrated Kendal green. See cuts under ''Cytisus'' and ''Genista.''}}

'''2.''' A besom, or brush with a long handle, for sweeping floors, etc.: so called from being originally made of the broom-plant. {{smaller|Brooms are now made in Europe of this and various other materials and in the United States their manufacture from broom-corn is an important business. A broom at the masthead of a vessel indicates that she is for sale, a sign derived}}

{{smaller|probably from the old habit of displaying boughs at shops and taverns.—'''Butcher’s broom''', a prickly liliaceous shrub, ''Ruscus aculeatus'': so called from its use by butchers in Europe in sweeping their blocks. Also called ''knee holly''.—'''Yellow broom''', a name sometimes given in the United States to the wild indigo, ''Baptisia tinctoria''.}}

'''broom<sup>1</sup>''' (bröm), ''v. t.'' [< ''broom''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] To sweep or clear away, as with a broom.
{{smaller block|The poor old workpeople ''brooming'' away the fallen leaves.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Newcomes, lviii.}}}}

'''broom<sup>2</sup>''' (bröm), ''v. t.'' Same as ''bream''<sup>2</sup>.

'''broom-brush''' (bröm′brush), ''n.'' A whisk-broom or clothes-brush made from broom-corn. [U. S.]

'''broom-bush''' (bröm′bu̇sh), ''n.'' A weedy annual composite, ''Parthenium Hysterophorus'', of tropical America.

'''broom-corn''' (bröm′kôrn), ''n.'' A variety of ''Sorghum vulgare'', a tall reed-like grass, rising to a height of 8 or 10 feet, a native of India. {{smaller|The branched panicles are made into brooms and brushes, for which purpose the plant is largely cultivated in the United States. The seed is used as feed for cattle.}}

'''broom-grass''' (bröm′gräs), ''n.'' '''1.''' Same as ''brome-grass''.—'''2.''' In the United States, some species of ''Andropogon'', as ''A. scoparius'' and ''A. macrourus''. Also called ''broom-sedge''.

'''broom-head''' (bröm′hed), ''n.'' An adjustable clasp for holding bunches of broom-corn to a broom-handle.

'''broom-rape''' (bröm′rāp), ''n.'' A name given to parasitic leafless plants of the genus ''Orobanche''

'''brooze†''', ''v.'' Same as ''browse''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Brora beds.''' See ''bed''<sup>1</sup>.

'''brose'''<sup>1</sup> (brōz), ''n.'' [Sc., < Gael. ''brothas'' (''th'' silent), brose. Cf. ''broose'', ''broth''.] A Scotch dish, made by pouring boiling water, boiling milk, the liquid in which meat has been boiled, or the like, on oatmeal, barley-meal, or other meal, and immediately mixing the ingredients by stirring. {{smaller|The dish is denominated from the nature of the liquid: as, ''kail-brose'', ''water-brose'', ''beef-brose'', etc.—'''Athole brose''', honey and whisky mixed together in equal parts, used in many parts of Scotland as a cure for hoarseness and sore throat arising from a cold. In the Highlands oatmeal is sometimes substituted for the honey. So called from Athole, a district of Perthshire, Scotland.}}

'''brose'''<sup>2</sup>'''†''', ''v.'' An obsolete Middle English form of ''bruise''.

'''brosely''' (brōz′li), ''n.'' [So called from the town of ''Brosely'' in Shropshire, where there was a large manufactory of pipes.] A tobacco-pipe. [Local, Eng.]

'''Brosimum''' (brō′si-mum), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. βρώσιμος, eatable, < βρῶσις, food, equiv. to βρῶμα, food: see ''broma''.] A genus of ''Urticaceæ'', suborder ''Artocarpeæ'', one species of which, ''B. Galactodendron'', is the cow-tree of South America. {{smaller|''B. Alicastrum'', the breadnut-tree, common in the woods of Jamaica, produces nuts which when roasted are used as bread, and taste like hazel-nuts. The wood resembles mahogany, and is sometimes used by cabinet-makers. The leaves and young branches form a most useful fattening fodder for cattle. The snake- or leopard-wood, used as veneers and for walking-canes, is yielded by a species, ''B. Aubletii'', from British Guiana.}}

'''Brosmiidæ''' (bros-mī′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Brosmius'' + ''-idæ.''] A family of anacanthine fishes, typified by the genus ''Brosmius:'' same as the subfamily ''Brosmiinæ.'' Also ''Brosmidæ.''

'''Brosmiinæ''' (bros-mi-ī′nē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Brosmius'' + ''-inæ.''] A subfamily of gadoid fishes, typified by the genus ''Brosmius'', and distinguished by the development of only one long dorsal and anal fin and the separation therefrom of the caudal. Also ''Brosminæ.''

'''Brosmius''' (bros′mi-us), ''n.'' [NL., < Icel. ''brosma'' = Norw. ''brosme'', the vernacular name of the ''Brosmius brosme.''] A genus of fishes belonging to the cod family, ''Gadidæ.'' {{smaller|One species, found on the northern coast of Scotland, is commonly called the ''torsk'' or ''tusk.'' See ''torsk.''}}

'''brosten†''', ''pp.'' A Middle English form of ''burst'', past participle of ''burst.''

'''brosy''' (brō′zi), ''a.'' [< ''brose''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Like brose; semifluid. [Scotch.]

'''brotany''' (brot′a-ni), ''n.'' [A short form (like equiv. AS. ''prūtene'') of ML. ''abrotanum:'' see ''abrotanum.''] Southernwood.

'''brotch''' (broch), ''v. t.'' [Perhaps a var. of the equiv. ''brath'', which is appar. < Icel. ''bregdha'', braid, knot, twine, = AS. ''bregdan'', E. ''braid''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.] To plait straw ropes round (a stack of corn). ''Jamieson.'' [Scotch.]

'''brotel†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''brittle.''

'''brotelness†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''brittleness.''

'''brot-ground''' (brot′ground), ''n.'' [< *''brot'', ult. < AS. ''broten'', pp. of ''breótan'', break (see ''brott''), +

''brothel''<sup>1</sup>.] A house of lewdness; a house appropriated to the purposes of prostitution; a bawdy-house; a stew.
{{smaller block|<poem>Epicurism and lust
Make it more like a tavern or a ''brothel'',
Than a grac’d palace.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 4.}}}}

'''brothel<sup>2</sup>†''' (broth′el), ''v. i.'' [< ''brothel''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' Cf. ''bordel'', ''n.''] To haunt brothels. ''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas.

'''brotheler†, brotheller†''' (broth′el-ėr), ''n.'' [< ''brothel''<sup>2</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''bordeler.''] One who frequents brothels.
{{smaller block|Gamesters, jockies, ''brothellers'' impure. {{right|''Cowper'', Task, ii.}}}}

'''brothel-house†''' (broth′el-hous), ''n.'' A brothel.

'''brotheller†''', ''n.'' See ''brotheler.''

'''brothelry†''' (broth′el-ri), ''n.'' [< ''brothel''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ry.''] '''1.''' A brothel.—'''2.''' Lewdness; obscenity.
{{smaller block|''Brothelry'' able to violate the ear of a pagan.{{right|''B. Jonson'', Ded. of Volpone.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|brook|695|brother}}</noinclude>also ''fruit'', ''fructify'', etc.] '''1†.''' To use; enjoy; have the full employment of.
{{smaller block|So mot I ''brouke'' wel myn eyen twaye.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Nun’s Priest’s Tale, l. 479.}}}}
'''2†.''' To earn; deserve.
{{smaller block|Which name she ''brooked'' as well for her proportion and grace as for the many happy voyages she made in her Majesty’s service.
{{right|''Sir R. Hawkins'', Voyage to the South Sea, p. 11.}}}}
'''3.''' To bear; endure; support; put up with: always in a negative sense.
{{smaller block|Your son, sir, insulted me in a manner which my honour could not ''brook''.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Rivals, v. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|They could ill ''brook'' the slightest indignity at his hand.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., Int.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To leisurely delights and sauntering thoughts
That ''brook'' no ceiling narrower than the blue.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Under the Willows.}}}}

'''brook-fish''' (bru̇k′fish), ''n.'' A fish of the family ''Cyprinodontidæ'' and genus ''Fundulus'': same as ''killifish'' and ''mummychog''. [Local, U. S.]

'''brookite''' (bru̇k′īt), ''n.''   [After Henry James ''Brooke'', an English crystallographer (1771–1857).]   One of the three forms in which titanium dioxid occurs in nature. {{smaller|It is found in orthorhombic crystals of a brown or yellow color to black, and adamantine to metallic luster. ''Jurinite'' is another name for the same mineral. ''Arkansite'' is an iron-black variety from Magnet Cove, Arkansas.}}

'''brooklet''' (bru̇k′let), ''n.''   [< ''brook''<sup>1</sup> + dim. ''-let''.]   A small brook.   ''Longfellow.''

'''brooklime''' (bru̇k′līm), ''n.''   [< ME. ''broklemp'', ''broklembe'', ''broklympe'', < ''brok'', brook, + ''lemp'', etc.; of obscure origin.]   A plant, ''Veronica Beccabunga'', with blue flowers in loose lateral spikes. See ''Veronica''.

'''brook-mint''' (bru̇k′mint), ''n.''   [< AS. ''brōcminte'', < ''brōc'', brook, + ''minte'', mint.]   The water-mint, ''Mentha sylvestris.''

'''broom-head''' (bröm′hed), ''n.'' An adjustable clasp for holding bunches of broom-corn to a broom-handle.

'''broom-rape''' (bröm′rāp), ''n.'' A name given to parasitic leafless plants of the genus ''Orobanche'' and in the United States to species of the similar allied genera ''Phelipæa'' and ''Aphyllon''. See ''Orobanchaceæ''.

'''broom-root''' (bröm′röt), ''n.'' A root exported from Mexico and used in the manufacture of brushes. {{smaller|It is supposed to be the root of a grass, also known in trade as ''Mexican'' or ''French whisk''.}}

'''broom-sedge''' (bröm′sej), ''n.'' Same as ''broom-grass''.

'''broomstaff''' (bröm′ståf), ''n.'' Same as ''broomstick''.

'''broomstick''' (bröm′stik), ''n.'' The stick or handle of a broom.

'''broom-tree''' (bröm′trē), ''n.'' A shrubby composite, ''Baccharis scoparia'', of the mountains of Jamaica, broom-like from its slender, densely crowded, almost leafless branchlets.

'''broom-vise''' (bröm′vīs), ''n.'' A clamping arrangement for flattening and holding broom-corn so that it can be sewed into brooms.

'''broomweed''' (bröm′wēd), ''n.'' A species of ''Corchorus'', ''C. siliquosus'', of tropical America, used for making brooms. {{smaller|The ''sweet broomweed'' of the tropics is a common weed, ''Scoparia dulcis'', of the natural order ''Scrophulariaceæ''.}}

'''broomy''' (brö′mi), ''a.''   [< ''broom''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Pertaining to or consisting of broom; bearing broom: as, a “''broomy'' peak,” ''J. Baillie.''

He who first reached the house was said to ''win the broose'', that is, the ''brose'', the prize of spice-broth allotted to the victor.   ''Jamieson.'' See ''brose''<sup>1</sup>.}}

'''brooze†''', ''v.'' Same as ''browse''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Brora beds.''' See ''bed''<sup>1</sup>.

See ''torsk.''}}

'''brot-ground''' (brot′ground), ''n.''   [< *''brot'', ult. < AS. ''broten'', pp. of ''breótan'', break (see ''brott''), + ''ground.'']   Ground newly broken up. [Prov. Eng.]

'''broth'''<sup>1</sup> (brôth), ''n.''   [< ME. ''broth'', < AS. ''broth'' = Icel. ''brodh'' = OHG. ''brot'', ''brod'' (> ML. ''brodum'', ''brodium'', > It. ''brodo'', ''broda'' = Sp. Pg. ''brodio'' = Pr. ''bro'' = OF. *''brou'', pl. ''broues'', > ME. ''browes'', > E. ''brewis'', q. v.), broth; cf. Ir. ''broth'' = Gael. ''brot'', broth, Gael. ''brothas'', brose (see ''brose''<sup>1</sup>); prob. (with formative ''-th'') from the root (*''bru'') of ''brew''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.]   Liquor in which flesh is boiled and macerated, usually with certain vegetables to give it a better relish. {{smaller|In Scotland the name is seldom used except when pot-barley forms one of the ingredients.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Good ''broth'', with good keeping, do much now and then;
Good diet, with wisdom, best comforteth men.</poem>
{{right|''Tusser.''}}}}

'''broth'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''a.'' See ''brath.''

'''brothel'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''n.''   [ME., also ''brethel'' (and corruptly ''brodel'', ''brodelle''), a wretch, a depraved man or woman; der. ''bretheling'', a wretch; < AS. *''breóthan'', only in comp. ''ā-breóthan'', ruin, frustrate, pp. ''ābrothen'', degenerate, base, trifling; connections doubtful.]   A wretch; a depraved person; a lewd man or woman.
{{smaller block|<poem>For nou is vche boye bold, ''brothel'' and other,
To talken of the trinite to beon holden a syre.</poem>

'''brothel'''<sup>2</sup> (broth′el), ''n.''   [An early mod. E. corruption of ME. ''bordel'', a house of ill-fame, by confusion with ME. ''brothel'', a wretch: see ''brothel''<sup>1</sup>.]   A house of lewdness; a house appropriated to the purposes of prostitution; a bawdy-house; a stew.
{{smaller block|<poem>Epicurism and lust
Make it more like a tavern or a ''brothel'',
Than a grac’d palace.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 4.}}}}

'''brothel<sup>2</sup>†''' (broth′el), ''v. i.''   [< ''brothel''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' Cf. ''bordel'', ''n.'']   To haunt brothels.   ''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas.

'''brotheler†, brotheller†''' (broth′el-ėr), ''n.''   [< ''brothel''<sup>2</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''bordeler.'']   One who frequents brothels.
{{smaller block|Gamesters, jockies, ''brothellers'' impure. {{right|''Cowper'', Task, ii.}}}}

'''brothel-house†''' (broth′el-hous), ''n.'' A brothel.

'''brotheller†''', ''n.'' See ''brotheler.''

'''brothelry†''' (broth′el-ri), ''n.''   [< ''brothel''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ry.'']   '''1.''' A brothel.—'''2.''' Lewdness; obscenity.
{{smaller block|''Brothelry'' able to violate the ear of a pagan.{{right|''B. Jonson'', Ded. of Volpone.}}}}

''bretheren, brethren'', formed, with weak pl. ending ''-en'', from ''brether, brethre, brithere'', also pl., an umlauted form of AS. ''brōthru'', also ''brōthor'', the usual pl. of ''brōthor;'' cf. AS. dat. sing. ''brēther''.]   '''1.''' A male person, in his relation to another person or other persons of either sex born of the same parents; a male relative in the first degree of descent or mutual kinship: used also of the lower animals: the converse of ''sister''. See ''brother-in-law'' and ''half-brother''.

{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' A male person in his relation to any other person or persons of the same blood or ancestry; a member of a common family or race in his relation to all other members; in the plural,<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
